processing: Not a single production method: kok choy simply means green tea in Uzbek, and it is an ordinary dried green leaf, packed in Uzbekistan from imported tea since the country grows none of its own.
harvest_season: No harvest of its own, since the leaf is imported and picked wherever it was grown. Buyers go by grade number rather than by season.
appearance_dry: Typically dark olive, twisted, somewhat coarse everyday leaf with some stalk, as is usual for mass-market green tea.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear yellow to light amber-green, deepening quickly in a long steep.
appearance_wet: Typically mid-sized olive leaves and pieces rather than whole buds.
taste_profile: Generally plain, refreshing and a little astringent, with toasted green notes and more grip the longer it sits in the pot.

brewing.notes: Rinse a round ceramic or clay pot with boiling water and steep 5 to 10 minutes; some people pour back and forth between pot and bowl during the steep. Fill the piala only a little so it is sipped hot. Brew a fresh pot rather than topping up a used one.

vintage_note: Sold by grade, not by vintage. The number comes from a Soviet-era scale said to run from No. 10 to No. 125, and No. 95 is the everyday tea most people drink. There is no harvest year on the pack in the usual sense, so buy from a recent batch and use it up as you would any green tea.
description:
Kok choy is less a named tea than a whole habit: it is the Uzbek for green tea, the cup that comes out before the food and stays through plov and shashlik. Uzbekistan's climate rules out plantations, so the leaf comes from abroad and gets packed in cities such as Tashkent and Samarkand.

The tea itself is simple. Little is recorded about how any given lot is made beyond what is usual for mass-market green tea, and retail packs of the popular No. 95 are sometimes described as Chinese green tea. Treat the grade number as the identity, not a place.

The character comes from the way it is served. A round pot, a long steep of 5 to 10 minutes and small sips from a piala give a hot, fairly brisk and cleansing cup, which is why people value it in summer heat and after fatty food. Lemon turns up, especially in winter; milk rarely does. Do not stretch a pot with more hot water: finish it, throw out the leaf and start again.

The piala is filled only to the bottom and handed back for another small pour, so the host keeps the tea hot and the guest keeps coming back. If you want to try it properly, look for a Central Asian grocer's No. 95 rather than a fine Chinese green, and brew it in the same long way.
history:
Green tea is the everyday drink across Uzbekistan, though black tea, qora choy, is also widely drunk and one cultural guide names it as the favourite in Tashkent. The numbered grades that buyers still use are said to go back to Soviet classification.

Little is documented about when kok choy became the default, or about where the leaf behind each grade has come from over time.
